title: Autostorager manual
what: It watches one folder and hands every G-code or bgcode file that appears in it to the server's storage. There the file is treated like a manual upload: the server reads its slicer details, draws its preview and lists it under Storage. The module never writes into the storage directly; it goes through the same API an upload uses. Only regular files are taken; a symbolic link is skipped.
flow1: The folder is read every few seconds, and only regular .gcode and .bgcode files are taken.
flow2: A file is read only after its size held still across two checks, so a file a slicer is still writing is left alone.
flow3: The module asks the storage for a free name and adds -1, -2 and so on if the name is taken.
flow4: The bytes are copied into the storage. Only after that copy is committed is the source moved into successful/.
flow5: A file that cannot be imported is moved into failed/, and a text file beside it says at which step it stopped and why.
linuxTitle: The folder on the server host, with PCL in a container
linux: A container sees only what is mounted into it. Create the folder on the server host, add it as a volume to the server's compose file, and enter the path inside the container on the settings page, not the host path. Then share the host folder as described above; the clients write into the same folder.
linuxPath: In the example the host folder /srv/autostorager appears as /incoming in the container, so the setting is /incoming. Mount as many host folders as you want to supervise, up to four. The module creates successful/ and failed/ inside each supervised folder; on the host they appear as /srv/autostorager/successful and /srv/autostorager/failed.
other: There the server is a normal process and the folder is read directly. Enter the full path, such as C:\Autostorager or /Users/you/Autostorager. No mount is involved.
settingFolder: Supervised folders: up to four absolute paths, added with [+] New supervised directory. Each folder is watched on its own and keeps its own successful/ and failed/. No folder means nothing is watched.
settingInterval: Check interval in seconds: how often the folder is read. 60 s is one minute. A very short interval means constant requests, which costs I/O on a network share; five seconds is enough for most folders, and a file is noticed within about one interval.
settingStorage: Storage: which storage instance the file is imported into. Most servers have one, called local.
settingSize: Largest file in megabytes, 250 by default. A larger file is not imported; it goes to failed/ with the reason.
settingMove: Move on success: when on, the source is moved into successful/ after the import. When off, it stays where it was, and the next check would import it again under a new name.
names: A name already present in the storage is never overwritten. The module tries the same name with -1, then -2, and so on until the storage answers that the name is free.
failed: The source goes to failed/, and beside it a file named <file>-failure.txt names the step, the reason, the time and the path. The same line appears under Recent imports on the settings page.
precedence: The settings page and the module's own dashboard page can both carry these values. What is saved on the settings page wins, because it is stored in the module's database and survives a restart. Saving the page takes operator rights on the module; a read-only user sees the values but cannot change them.
check: Drop a small .gcode into the folder. Within about one interval it should disappear from there, appear as successful/ inside the folder, and show up under Storage in the server with its preview. The Recent imports list on the settings page tells the same story.
smbTitle: The easy way: a folder on the server, mounted on your computer
smb: Create a folder on the server and share it. Mount that share on your computer, where it appears as a normal drive or folder: Y: on Windows, /mnt/y on Linux, smb://server/share on macOS. Enter the server path of that folder here, then save your prints into it from the slicer. The module imports them from there and moves them into successful/ inside the same share. If the server runs in a container, enter the path inside the container, not the host path.
localTitle: PCL and the folder on the same computer
local: If PCL runs on the same computer as the folder, one directory is enough. Create it, enter its path, and save your prints into it. Nothing is shared and nothing is mounted.
pathTitle: What to enter as the supervised folder
path: The field takes the path as the server sees it, not as your computer sees it. Without a container that is the folder itself, such as /srv/autostorager. In a container it is the path inside the container. In this example /app/config/pc-in is a container path: the host folder is pc-in inside the server's config directory, and that directory is mounted into the container as /app/config. Your own folders and mount points are your own; what matters is that the path exists where the container looks. Your computer's drive letter or /mnt path is never the value to enter here.
picture1: 1. Export from the slicer into the network drive.
picture3: 3. Enter that folder on this page, as the server sees it.
picture5: 5. With its slicer details and preview.
hostSettingsTitle: The settings in the extension's Settings tab
hostSettings: The server keeps a Settings tab for every extension. It carries the same values as this page and two more: language and message. What is saved on the Autostorager page wins, because it is stored in the module's database. The tab itself is for operators; a read-only user cannot change its fields.
hostLanguage: language: system follows the browser, or en, de or cs. The language section below explains it.
hostMessage: message: the line the module's own route answers with. It is not drawn on the page; leave it unless a tool reads the route.
hostDefaults: interval_seconds, storage, max_mb, move_on_success: the defaults the module starts with. The values saved on the Autostorager page win.
captionSettings: The Settings tab of Autostorager on the server, with language, message and the other defaults.
language: The language is set on the server, not on this page: Extensions, Autostorager, Settings, the field language. system means the language the browser asks for; en, de or cs pin one. Czech is cs, not cz, though a country code is accepted as a courtesy.
languageRestart: The choice is saved at once and read at start-up, so the module restarts when it is saved. Pick a quiet moment: an import halfway through is cut off by that restart. A language this package does not carry falls back to the browser's, and from there to English. The buttons above switch the language for this visit without saving anything.
languageContribute: Want your own language? Copy locales/en.json and manual/en.json to <tag>.json, translate the values, keep the keys, open a pull request. Nobody here should write a language they do not speak, and a machine translation reads like one. The Czech is exactly that: a trial balloon, translated by a machine. Whether it holds up is for Czech readers to say. The new file has to land on GitHub; a local copy does not ship.
rights: Prusa Connect Local keeps its own accounts. The first account created at setup is administrator of org:local. An administrator adds people under Settings > People; the role on the organization is written with the grant below. The server's root shell is not a PCL account.
rightsViewer: viewer: may read, not change. The Autostorager page is visible; Save answers 403.
rightsOperator: operator: may change the extension's settings; Save takes operate_resource on resource_kind:sink.
rightsAdmin: admin: the highest role on org:local; it includes operator.
rightsNote: Use admin instead of operator for admin rights. The id comes from Settings > People or the answer to POST /api/v1/auth/accounts. The call needs an administrator's session.
rightsSystems: The first account is created on the setup page from a code in the server log: docker logs for a container, journalctl -u for a service, or the console on macOS and Windows. The roles are the same on Linux, macOS and Windows. They live in the server's database, not in the operating system's users. On Windows the server may need to be started as Administrator to bind a port or reach a folder, but that does not make the browser account an admin; the PCL account and its role do. On Linux and macOS the server usually runs as a service user, and the watched folder has to be readable and writable by that user.
files: Only regular files are taken. The watcher reads the top level of each supervised folder and does not search subfolders. A symbolic link is skipped, even when its name ends in .gcode or .bgcode: it stays where it is and is not imported, moved or followed. A link can point at any file the server can read, so the watcher never follows one. The same applies to directories, devices, pipes and sockets. Replace the link with the file itself if it should be printed. The watcher never leaves the watched folder. If successful/ or failed/ is a link that points outside, the move is refused. A failure report is created new and is never written through an existing file or link.
remoteTitle: The folder stays on a client: share it and mount it on the server
remote: Use this when the folder must stay on a Windows, Linux or Mac client. Share the folder on the client, mount the share on the server, and add the mount path in Autostorager. This is more work: every client needs its own share, credentials and mount, and the client must be on. It is how the server watches a folder that physically lives on your home machine.
remoteSamba:
# Linux client: share the folder
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/g/Autostorager
sudo smbpasswd -a ulli

# /etc/samba/smb.conf:
[global]
   workgroup = WORKGROUP
   security = user
   map to guest = bad user
   server min protocol = SMB2

[autostorager]
   path = /mnt/g/Autostorager
   browseable = yes
   read only = no
   valid users = ulli
   force user = ulli
   create mask = 0664
   directory mask = 0775
   follow symlinks = no

sudo systemctl enable --now smb.service
remoteShare: If a firewall is active, allow Samba: sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=samba and sudo firewall-cmd --reload on firewalld, or sudo ufw allow Samba on ufw. Test the share from the server with smbclient -L 192.168.178.25 -U ulli.
remoteMount:
# On the PCL server:
sudo install -m 600 /dev/null /etc/samba/cred-autostorager
printf 'username=ulli\npassword=YOUR-SAMBA-PASSWORD\n' | sudo tee /etc/samba/cred-autostorager >/dev/null
sudo mkdir -p /home/ulli/connect-local/config/autostorager-g
sudo mount -t cifs //192.168.178.25/Autostorager \
  /home/ulli/connect-local/config/autostorager-g \
  -o credentials=/etc/samba/cred-autostorager,uid=0,gid=0,file_mode=0666,dir_mode=0777,vers=3.0
remoteFstab: Make it survive a reboot. Add this line to /etc/fstab, then run sudo systemctl daemon-reload and sudo mount -a. nofail and x-systemd.automount keep the server booting when the desktop is off; the folder appears when the desktop is on.
remoteAdd: In Autostorager, add the path inside the container, not the desktop path: /app/config/autostorager-g. It becomes a second supervised folder. Each folder has its own successful/ and failed/, and up to four can be watched. The files land in the same storage. The source is moved into successful/ on the desktop share after the import.
remoteNote: One mount per client, up to four. The client must be on and the share reachable; if it is off, the mount is missing and the module reports the folder as an error. Use a fixed address or a DHCP reservation. The module still takes only regular files at the top level; subfolders are ignored.
where: There are three setups. 1) PCL and the folder on the same computer: one directory, no share and no mount. 2) PCL on a server, the folder on the server: create one folder on the server, share it, and let every client machine send its files there. This is the recommended setup for a farm: one queue, one place to look. 3) PCL on a server, the folders stay on the clients: share each client folder and mount it on the server. This is more work, but it is how the server watches a folder that physically lives on a Windows, Linux or Mac machine. Up to four folders are supported. The sections below show all three.
serverTitle: PCL on a server: one folder on the server, shared with the clients
server: This is the usual choice when PCL runs on a server. Create the folder on the server host, make it visible in the PCL container, and share the host folder on the network. Every client mounts the share and writes into the same queue. Autostorager watches one folder; the clients need no PCL and no Autostorager, only the share. One queue is easier to explain and easier to back up than four client folders.
serverShare:
# On the PCL server host:
sudo mkdir -p /srv/autostorager
sudo chown -R ulli:ulli /srv/autostorager

# /etc/samba/smb.conf:
[autostorager]
   path = /srv/autostorager
   browseable = yes
   read only = no
   valid users = ulli
   force user = ulli
   create mask = 0664
   directory mask = 0775
   follow symlinks = no

sudo smbpasswd -a ulli
sudo systemctl enable --now smb.service
serverClients: On Windows, open \\SERVER\autostorager in Explorer and map it as a drive. On Linux, connect to smb://SERVER/autostorager or mount it with CIFS; on macOS, Finder > Go > Connect to Server, smb://SERVER/autostorager. Sign in with the Samba user and password. The container path for the same host folder is what you add in Autostorager; the next section shows the host-folder-to-container mapping.
remoteWindows: On Windows: right-click the folder, Properties > Sharing > Advanced Sharing. Share it as Autostorager, give the server's user read and write, and allow File and Printer Sharing for the private network in the firewall. The server mounts //WINDOWS-IP/Autostorager.
remoteMac: On macOS: System Settings > General > Sharing > File Sharing > Options. Enable Share files and folders using SMB, add the folder, and enable the user. The server mounts //MAC-IP/Autostorager.
